extracted.intended_audience: agency policymakers, administrative law scholars, and practitioners interested in public participation in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for citizens (and designers of public participation systems) on how to prepare effective public comments to agency rulemakings that overcome barriers of interest, expertise, and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate the commenter's specific stake/interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the commenter's stake (resident, worker, family member, profession) and indicate why the rule matters to the commenter specifically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the personal connection to the issue (who you are and how you are affected). Describe what the commenter has personally observed to show genuine engagement rather than abstract advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate for limited expertise through specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor comments to specific provisions and concrete facts rather than attempting broad policy arguments beyond the commenter's knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor to a specific paragraph or provision. Describe a concrete experience or impact. Avoid attempting to engage agency-wide policy debates beyond the commenter's knowledge or technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor to a specific provision of the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference and tie the comment to a particular paragraph, section, or provision in the rulemaking text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing to the precise text helps agencies locate and act on the comment; specificity increases credibility and usefulness compared with vague or general complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe a concrete experience or impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide factual, experience-based information about how a proposed rule would affect the commenter or others in particular circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples, incidents, or measurable impacts rather than abstract assertions. This helps compensate for technical gaps and provides evidence agencies can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engaging beyond your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from trying to debate complex technical or agency-wide policy issues unless you have the relevant subject-matter knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack technical expertise, focus on specific, factual, experiential input. Overreaching into broad policy arguments reduces credibility and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate for limited time through focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Because drafting substantive comments takes time, effective comments typically concentrate on a single clear point rather than covering many issues shallowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a single, clear request and provide one well-developed factual basis. Focused comments are more likely to be substantive and read by agency staff; resist the temptation to try to fix every problem in one submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a single, clear request
rubrics_metrics.description: State one concrete change or action you want the agency to take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A focussed ask (e.g., change wording in §X, add requirement Y) is more actionable than multiple or vague requests. This helps agencies translate comments into rule edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide one well-developed factual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Support your primary request with a single, well-documented factual example or piece of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth over breadth: a thoroughly explained factual example is more persuasive and usable than many unsubstantiated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist boilerplate or mass-campaign text
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid copying and pasting generic advocacy language or mass-comment templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique, tailored comments are more likely to be considered substantive. Mass-produced boilerplate is less useful and may be discounted by agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the comment shows you have read the proposal (not just an advocacy summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate engagement with the actual proposed rule text rather than a secondhand advocacy summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to specific sections, accurate citations of proposal language, or discussion of concrete provisions show that the commenter has read the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the comment unique in voice and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide original perspective, wording, or facts that distinguish the submission from mass-campaign comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal anecdotes, localized impacts, or professional observations increase distinctiveness. Avoid generic slogans and identical phrasing used by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should provide plain-language summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should supply clear, accessible summaries of proposals to lower information barriers to participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain-language summaries help citizens identify relevance and reduce the 'interest' barrier by making complex proposals more approachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should provide structured comment forms eliciting specific information
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured forms that ask for particular facts or link comments to provisions can prompt more useful, specific submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms that elicit stake, affected provision, and concrete evidence can help overcome expertise and time barriers by guiding commenters to produce actionable input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should provide feedback to commenters about how comments were used
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should inform participants about the influence of comments to sustain engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback increases perceived payoff for participation and can motivate future contributions; without feedback, participation may decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should engage with diverse formats (narrative, video, in-person testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should accept and integrate a variety of submission formats to broaden participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing narratives, videos, and in-person testimony accommodates different communicative strengths and can help include participants who struggle with written technical comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume technology alone will democratize rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution that online dockets and portals by themselves are insufficient to improve participation quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology can increase access, but substantive participation still depends on interest, expertise, and time; agencies must pair technology with substantive supports (summaries, structured prompts, feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the three underlying obstacles: interest, expertise, time
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective participation requires addressing awareness/relevance (interest), subject-matter knowledge (expertise), and the time required to prepare substantive comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interventions and individual comment strategies with these three barriers in mind: increase awareness, lower technical barriers, and reduce time costs through structure and guidance.
